Two tables go in per modality: a feature-by-sample matrix of measurements, and a sample table with
one row per sample. Nothing about the organism, the assay or the condition is assumed, and no column
name beyond the two below is required.

The modalities are measured on different individuals, so what connects them is a fixed vocabulary of
named biological concepts rather than a shared sample. A concept is a set of features that belong
together for a stated biological reason, and every modality is scored on the same concepts. A
modality therefore has to supply two things: measurements its samples can be compared on, and
feature identifiers that reach the vocabulary.

## The container the tables become

`chorale_load()` puts the two tables into a
[SummarizedExperiment](https://bioconductor.org/packages/SummarizedExperiment), which is the
container every later step reads:

```r
se <- chorale_load(matrix, samples)
SummarizedExperiment::assay(se)    # the measurements
SummarizedExperiment::colData(se)  # the sample table
```

This is Bioconductor's standard structure for a feature-by-sample assay with its sample annotation,
and using it has three consequences. The measurements and the sample table are one object, so they
cannot be subset, reordered or filtered out of alignment with one another. Feature and sample
identifiers stay bound to the numbers rather than living in a separate vector. And a study whose
data already sit in a `SummarizedExperiment` is in the right shape, as is one using a subclass such
as a `DESeqDataSet` or a `SingleCellExperiment`:

```r
se <- chorale_load(SummarizedExperiment::assay(existing),
                   as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(existing)))
```

`chorale_load()` is the route in because it also resolves the design labels into one vocabulary, as
described below. An object built by hand can be passed to `chorale_concept_fit()` directly, provided
its `colData` already carries the required columns in canonical form.

## The measurement matrix

Features in rows, samples in columns, and `colnames(matrix)` equal to `samples$sample_id` in the
same order. A modality is whatever was measured on its own set of samples: a transcriptome, a
proteome, a lipidome, a panel of variant dosages. Each is one matrix and one call.

Row names are the feature identifiers, and they are what reaches the vocabulary of concepts. Gene
and protein modalities are mapped to Entrez identifiers by
[`chorale_map()`](https://lescailab.github.io/chorale/reference/chorale_map),
from Ensembl identifiers, symbols or UniProt accessions. A lipidome is declared with
`feature_space = "lipid"` and reaches the same concepts through its class names instead.

How many features a modality has for a concept decides whether it can be scored on that concept at
all. `chorale_concepts()` reports that count for every concept and every modality, so a modality
whose annotation reaches little of the vocabulary is visible before anything is fitted rather than
afterwards as an absence of results.

Missing values are permitted. Each feature is centred and scaled before decomposition, and an entry
that is not finite afterwards is set to the feature mean, so a feature observed in few samples
contributes little and adds noise in its place. Filter on detection rate before loading.

## The scale each matrix is on

Two different jobs are involved, and only the second is done for you.

**Between samples.** Samples must already be comparable within the modality, because standardisation
acts on a feature across samples and cannot remove a difference in library size or in total ion
current. Apply the modality's own normalisation first: size factors, CPM or TPM for sequencing
counts, total-intensity or median scaling for mass spectrometry.

**Within a feature.** The measurement scale is read from the matrix, so no particular unit is
required. `transform = "auto"`, the default, chooses per modality:

| What the matrix holds | Applied | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Integer counts spanning orders of magnitude: raw sequencing counts, spectral counts | `vst` | Under Anscombe's transform a Poisson variance no longer grows with the mean, so a highly expressed feature stops dominating an axis for no biological reason. |
| Positive continuous values, right-skewed: TPM, FPKM, RPKM, normalised LFQ intensities, peak areas | `log` | Label-free intensities span orders of magnitude. `log1p` is used, which keeps zeros finite. |
| Values already on a symmetric scale: log ratios, log intensities, z-scores, variant dosages | `none` | Already symmetric, and a further transform would distort it. |

The rule is mechanical. Any negative value means the matrix is already on a symmetric scale and
nothing is applied. Otherwise, whole numbers whose 99th percentile exceeds five times their median
take the variance-stabilising transform; a skewness above one with the same spread takes the
logarithm; anything else is left alone. What was applied is recorded in the fit.

Where the matrix is not what its distribution suggests, say it explicitly, one value per modality:

```r
fit <- chorale_concept_fit(containers, sets,
                           transform = c(RNA = "vst", PROT = "log", METAB = "none"))
```

## What every modality must carry

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sample_id` | Unique across the collection, and matching the matrix column names in order. |
| `phenotype` | The contrast being estimated, on at least two levels. |

The phenotype is a condition of entry rather than a covariate. The estimand is a contrast, so a
modality that cannot express one cannot contribute to it, and a run whose modalities do not all
carry it stops with that named as the reason.

The identifier has to be unique across the whole collection and not only within a modality, since
the design stands in for matched individuals only where there are none.
`chorale_check_disjoint()` reports every identifier carried by more than one modality, and
`chorale_concept_fit()` and `chorale_gates()` run it and warn. The warning does not stop the run:
two independent studies can give one name to two individuals, and only the analyst can say which
of the two a collision is.

The column need not literally be called `phenotype`. Its role and reference
level are analysis settings:

```r
control <- chorale_control(
  phenotype_column = "outcome",
  phenotype_reference = "reference"
)
fit <- chorale_concept_fit(containers, sets, control = control)
```

The phenotype may be any estimable categorical comparison: treatment response,
exposure group, genotype class, time category, or another study-defined outcome.
Every modality must contain the declared reference and at least one comparison
level.

## What every other column does

Every remaining column is a possible covariate. Eligible covariates enter the model the concept
score is regressed on, so the reported phenotype effect is adjusted for them. Excluded covariates
are reported with a reason: absent modality, incompatible type or levels, excessive missingness, or
lack of joint estimability.

How a covariate is read follows from its type in the sample table, so the type is what needs getting
right.

| Stored as | Read as | What it contributes |
|---|---|---|
| Character or factor | Categorical | One adjusted coefficient per level beyond a common reference, on the levels every modality realises. |
| Numeric in every modality | Continuous | One adjusted slope after the covariate is standardised. |
| A number stored as text | Categorical | The values become levels, so two cohorts recording the same age as `6` and `6.0` share none. A continuous covariate stored as text is read this way, which is the common mistake. |

The design is read as supplied. A study that wants a continuous covariate treated in bands supplies
the bands as a column of their own, which keeps the choice of cut points with the person who knows
what they mean.

Two column names are treated as bookkeeping rather than biology and never anchor a comparison:
`sample_id` and `modality`. A column holding a distinct value for nearly every sample identifies
the sample rather than grouping it, and is dropped for the same reason.

## One set of words for the design labels

Cohorts assembled by different groups can record the same thing differently. CHORALE maps only
unambiguous general labels, such as `ctrl` to `control` and `male` to `M`. Study-specific meanings
are never guessed.

Labels are therefore resolved as the data are read.

| Covariate | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `phenotype` | `case`, `control` |
| `sex` | `F`, `M` |
| `genotype` | `carrier`, `non-carrier` |

The registry holds only terms general across biology. Names particular to one organism, model or
study are absent by design, since a tool carrying the labels of the data it was built on fits
nothing else. A study whose labels are not covered supplies its own:

```r
registry <- chorale_label_registry()
registry$phenotype <- c(registry$phenotype, "study_case" = "case")
registry$treatment <- c("drug" = "treated", "placebo" = "untreated")
se <- chorale_load(matrix, design, labels = registry)
```

A label the registry does not recognise is left as it is. Two cohorts using different unrecognised
labels for the same thing share no level, which is a silent way to recover nothing, so
`chorale_check_design()` reports what a collection can and cannot anchor on before anything is
fitted.

## Genotype beside phenotype

Where a design records genotype separately from phenotype status, the phenotype remains the contrast
being estimated and genotype enters as one more covariate the effect is adjusted for. A study whose
primary contrast *is* the genotype puts it in the `phenotype` column, since that column names the
role rather than the measurement.

## Organism and annotation

Nothing in the estimator is tied to an organism. Gene identifiers are mapped through whichever
Bioconductor annotation the study needs, and the curated vocabulary is retrieved for whichever
species it describes.

```r
# Mouse-native collections and mouse annotation.
mouse_map <- chorale_map(rownames(matrix), from = "ENSEMBL",
                         orgdb = "org.Mm.eg.db")
mouse_sets <- chorale_genesets(species = "Mus musculus", db_species = "MM")

# Human collections and human annotation.
feature_map <- chorale_map(rownames(matrix), from = "ENSEMBL",
                           orgdb = "org.Hs.eg.db")
sets <- chorale_genesets(species = "Homo sapiens", db_species = "HS")
```

Another annotated organism uses its Bioconductor `OrgDb`. Curated collections
can come from a compatible source database or be supplied as custom Entrez sets:

```r
other_map <- chorale_map(rownames(matrix), from = "SYMBOL",
                         orgdb = "org.Species.eg.db")
custom_sets <- list(
  concept_a = c("101", "102", "103", "104", "105"),
  concept_b = c("201", "202", "203", "204", "205")
)
sets <- chorale_genesets(collections = character(), custom = custom_sets,
                         min_size = 5)
```

The vocabulary is an argument, so a collection can be analysed in curated pathways, in cell type
signatures, in a set of concepts defined for the study, or in any combination of them. What the
vocabulary contains bounds what the concept channel can express, which is why it is chosen before
the data are looked at.

The lipid-to-pathway table takes its compound annotation from one organism, but it is keyed on set
names that are the same across species. A lipid is therefore placed in the set a study of any
organism would use, wherever that pathway exists in it. A table of the same shape built for another
organism is supplied in its place.

## Conditions on what is supplied

Matrices are normalised within each modality before they are loaded. A cross-modal transformation
that uses the intended answer, or constructed sample pairs, puts information into the scores that
the design is then asked to find in them, so scoring must see each modality on its own. Batch and
study variables belong in the design, where their effects are adjusted and reported.

## Shared covariates, local nuisance, and exchangeability

These three ideas are related but not interchangeable.

- A **shared covariate** is represented compatibly in every modality and enters
  the regression model for concept and joint evidence.
- A **modality-local nuisance variable** is recorded only for one modality. It
  can be removed from that modality's concept scores before joint stacking.
- An **exchangeability block** states which samples may exchange residuals under
  permutation. It describes sampling or dependence, not merely adjustment.

```r
state <- chorale_joint_state(
  fit$encoding,
  n_components = 2,
  nuisance = list(modality_a = c("local_batch", "processing_day"))
)

control <- chorale_control(
  exchangeability_blocks = c("subject_group", "processing_block")
)
```

Do not infer exchangeability blocks from every design column. A continuous age
column would create one-sample blocks and prevent meaningful permutation.
Declare only restrictions justified by the way observations were sampled or
processed. Missing nuisance values are not imputed: samples unavailable to the
local nuisance model retain their original score.

## Preflight checklist

Before fitting, verify that matrix columns match `sample_id`, the phenotype
contrast exists in every modality, numeric covariates are stored as numeric,
identifier mapping reaches the intended concepts, and all transformations and
normalisations are recorded. Run `chorale_check_design()` and
`chorale_check_disjoint()`, and inspect `chorale_concepts()$coverage`. These checks distinguish a weak biological signal
from a question the inputs never made estimable.
